body.objective: Students will be able to read rhythms in simple time.
body.iCan: I can read rhythms in simple time.
successCriteria: I can count and perform rhythms in 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4
I can read and write note and rest values
I can identify the time signature of a piece by ear
body.hook: Reading music is like reading a map of sound. Once you can count rhythms in simple time, you can sight-read a drum part, follow a guitar tab with rhythm, or play with any band. It all starts with a steady beat and knowing how long each note lasts.

study.title: Counting Time
study.question: How do I read and count rhythms in simple time?
study.passage:
Note values in 4/4: whole = 4 beats, half = 2, quarter = 1, eighth = ½, sixteenth = ¼, dotted half = 3, dotted quarter = 1½. Rests have the same values.
Time signatures: The top number is beats per bar; the bottom number shows which note gets one beat (4 = quarter note).
• 2/4: two beats per bar (marches)
• 3/4: three beats per bar (waltzes)
• 4/4: four beats per bar (most pop and rock)
Counting: quarter notes "1 2 3 4"; eighths "1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &"; sixteenths "1 e & a 2 e & a."
Part 1, Count and clap (10 minutes): Read 8 rhythm lines from the board, counting aloud.
Part 2, Feel the metre (10 minutes): Listen to four short clips (a march, a waltz, a rock song and a pop ballad). Find the strong beat and count to identify 2/4, 3/4 or 4/4.
Part 3, Write (10 minutes): Write four bars of 3/4 and four bars of 4/4 using at least one dotted note, one tie and one rest. Check each bar adds up.
Part 4, Perform (10 minutes): Perform your rhythm on body percussion or drums while a partner keeps the beat.
